articles.text: Piedmont City Council considered the naming of the triangle park at the intersection of Magnolia and Wildwood Avenues as “Dearing Family Memorial Park,” as a memorial to Sidney Dearing, Piedmont’s first black resident in 1924. City Administrator Sara Lillevand said more public input should be sought as the city seeks to address what is widely considered a blight on Piedmont’s past. Sidney and Irene Dearing were Piedmont’s first black homeowners. They purchased a home in 1924 and were driven out by a mob of white Piedmont residents. The Piedmont Police Department did little to help as a mob estimated at 500 people demanded the family’s removal. The City Council offered to purchase the home from the Dearing family but offered less than the family had originally paid, claiming that the property purchase was needed to construct a road between Wildwood and Fairview Avenues, a road that was never constructed. “I would suggest that we slow down on the name itself, and provide more opportunity for public engagement on this important effort,” Lillevand said. “I do believe the triangle park (at Wildwood and Magnolia) is an appropriate place to acknowledge and remember the Dearing family.” Rather than recommending to City Council that they approve the naming of the city park, Lillevand revised the agenda item to direct Park Commission to explore “and make recommendations to city council on opportunities to memorialize the Sidney Dearing family history.” The triangle park is across the street from the former Dearing home. Councilmember Jennifer Long, echoing Lillevand’s introduction, said that the renaming is meant to recognize this specific story and that the city would engage in other actions not specifically related to Dearing but to the goal of creating an inclusive community. Shelia Leuning, President of Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC), urged City Council to seek input directly from the Dearing family and descendants. Lois Corrin, a member of PADC, League of Woman Voters, and a Piedmont resident for over 30 years, offered comments on the next step. “I know we have the resources, the political will, and the social will to actually do something about this and perhaps lead by example for other communities,” she said. “I’m looking forward to this being a first step.” “This is a meaningful step on, not an end to, the journey to achieving the vision laid out by City Council in its anti-racism resolution,” Lillevand said.
articles.title: City to consider naming triangle park for Dearing family

Time for school board to start making sense By Margaret Moneypenny The Principals of PHS and PMS and Superintendent Booker are leaving PUSD. The principal replacements were found quickly. There is talk of hurriedly hiring an external Interim Superintendent to allow a new school board to hire the permanent replacement. This could cheat our children and schools. An Interim Superintendent passively holding steady to current momentum could become the default permanent choice. Since champion fundraisers of PEF win almost every school board seat, causing board groupthink, the new school board is unlikely to think any differently. Is there an heir apparent? Will a yearlong search merely yield another insider Superintendent? These risks were apparent in the 2011 rapid promotion of Booker to Assistant Superintendent and quick 2015 appointment to Superintendent. PUSD’s job description specified a Superintendent to “work effectively with a highly capable and dedicated [School] Board.’’ But Booker rubber stamped all wishes of the largest donors to the Ed Foundation even while calling out this “pay to play” system. Some shenanigans included refinancing school bonds to defer property taxes, backing an overpriced theater renovation designed by a large donor with no prior theater design experience (that voters struck down), expanding his roster of highly paid administrators at the expense of paying teachers a living wage, and taking curriculum decisions away from Department Chairs. Multiple scandals erupted in the local and national press from 2015 to 2022. Meanwhile, it became harder for graduates to get into their colleges of choice and visits to the Wellness Center by high school students skyrocketed. Early in Booker’s tenure, school board meetings were not well attended. Few knew that the school board was not leading or researching the issues or that Booker’s research was lacking or biased. These shortcomings became widely apparent during the pandemic with hundreds of parents attending school board meetings. The school’s response to the pandemic was Booker’s chance to shine. But instead, he burned bridges with parents, often refusing or failing to answer questions about his policies or overlooking the alternatives. District-wide enrollment declined from 2,708 in the 2015- 16 school year to 2,348 students in the 2022-22 school year. Of the 360-student decline, 219 left during the 2020-22 pandemic. Voters in 2020 ushered in school board members who took a back seat to Superintendent Booker, giving him a CEO title and apparently deferring to him. They also told him that DEI-B would be the primary lens through which he will govern the school district. Will any new Superintendent share the community’s views and expectations on Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging (DEI-B), educational excellence, and transparency in decision-making? articles.text: National Bike to Work Day, Friday, May 20, takes place at the conclusion of Bike to Wherever Days, which spans the entire month of May. The singular Bike to Work event has been one of the largest bicycle commute celebrations in the United States for over 20 years. Before the global pandemic began in 2020, it was a celebration of cycling as a healthy way to commute to work - during the pandemic and moving forward, the event was rebranded as “Bike to Wherever” in response to a large percentage of the Bay Area residents who began working remotely and did not commute. Bike to Work Day is bringing back “energizer” stations within all Bay Area counties. They are scattered across counties along ideal bike routes and paths - attendees are encouraged to stop by one of the locations and grab a commemorative tote bag and fill up their own reusable water bottles. To find an energizer station in the East Bay, visit https://bikeeastbay.org/find-your-energizer-station-bike-wherever-day-2022. To learn more about the event, or to sign up as a volunteer, visit https://bikeeastbay.org. No registration is required to participate, and tote bags will be available while supplies last.
articles.title: Bike to Work Day is May 20

articles.text: The New Wheel, an entrepreneurial Bay Area business focused on providing e-bikes to consumers, will open its first Oakland store with a Grand Opening this Sunday, May 22, at 1446 Leimert Boulevard near Rocky’s Market. It’s the third Bay Area e-bike shop opened by married couple Brett Thurber and Karen Wiener, whose vision for The New Wheel began more than a decade ago. “We began to realize the transformational nature of e-bikes for experiencing the richness of local life,” said Weiner. “At the same time, we understood it would take a lot of time and effort to proliferate this vision to the public. We are very pleased to open a new shop in Oakland and serve the community.” The couple find it inspiring to help bring positive change to so many individuals and families throughout the Bay Area, including an improved quality of life. It’s also gratifying for them to know that they are helping to better the environment and spur public policy decisions that support e-bikes as a highly beneficial means of transportation. Brett and Karen started their journey together at UC Berkeley. They opened their first e-bike shop in 2012 in the Bernal Heights neighborhood of San Francisco and a second location in Larkspur four years later. According to University of Tennessee Professor Chris Cherry, whose research focuses on e-bikes and other sustainable modes of transportation, the average cost of ownership, maintenance, and fuel for a car is about $8,000 per year. The average e-bike owner may spend $400 a year on those same expenses. An e-bike is a great way to reduce travel expenses and still have a lot of mobility. For the environment, cars - even EVs - emit 10-30 times more greenhouse gas emissions than e-bikes. “The electric bike has become a crowd-pleaser among cyclists and mobility and urban planning advocates who see it as a catalyst for building more bike infrastructure and addressing issues like traffic congestion,” said Professor Cherry. “It’s taking bicycling out of this very niche group of riders that are either Sunday riders or hard-core commuters and expanding it across the board.” The New Wheel’s mission is a labor of love that started with a fledgling idea more than a decade ago, followed by a tremendous amount of fortitude in the intervening years. In addition to supporting The New Wheel’s customers, Brett and Karen are proud to have created a positive, family-oriented work environment for bike professionals in service, sales and administration. The new store is located at 1446 Leimert Boulevard in the Oakmore neighborhood near Rocky’s Market. The public is invited to the Grand Opening this Saturday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. The event includes live music, food treats by Two Local Girls Catering and food trucks by Rocky’s Market. Jeremy Medina is store manager of The New Wheel in Oakland. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: In February 2021, the Piedmont City Council adopted reach codes that require energy efficiency measures to be included in new construction and existing building renovations. Reach codes are local amendments that go above and beyond existing California building codes (Title 24) to improve the energy efficiency of buildings and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The survey is live and will be open until May 20, 2022. All those who complete the online survey will be entered into a raffle to receive a sustainability prize. Take the Community Survey here (https://tinyurl. com/reachcodesurvey). For more information about the reach codes and additional community engagement opportunities, visit the City’s Reach Code Information webpage housed under the Planning & Building Department. articles.text: Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King had an accessory dwelling unit (ADU) delivered by Abodu and installed by crane in her backyard on Friday morning, May 4. It will be the new home of her father, Kenneth Gray. “He didn’t want to move to Rossmoor and he wasn’t interested in a senior apartment somewhere. So, we moved forward with the Abodu,” she said. Mayor King added that it has taken almost a year for the installation to be finalized, with the finishing touches of painting and technology hookups completed last week. Abodu is a full-service ADU company that oversees the entire process from backyard assessment, building permits, and installation. The entire process Mayor King speaks with an Abodu crew member on installation day, May 4. Pictured inside a new ADU in the backyard of Mayor Teddy Gray King are Kenneth Gray (left), Teddy King and dog Murphy, John Whitehurst, and Nicholas King, a high school freshman. Kenneth Gray, is welcomed to his new home in the backyard of his daughter, Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King. can take anywhere from six months to a year - construction of the ADU happens off-site, and once completed, the entire unit is crane-lifted onto the homeowner’s property which takes less than a day. The service is available through Northern and Southern California as well as the Pacific Northwest. The structure is a 500-square foot, one-bedroom unit with a base price of $242,000. It has a bedroom, built-in wardrobe, a full bathroom with shower, a full kitchen with dishwasher and sink, and a living room with a window bench. “It’s a big expenditure but a nice product,” noted King. “It can be a good option for people who need to develop more housing, as was my case.” In addition to installing the ADU, Abodu staff were on-site serving coffee and pastries to neighbors who came to see the unit being fitted by crane over the house and onto the backyard. This is the second Abodu ADU delivery in town, In July 2021, resident Jason Villaluz had a 340-square foot studio-style ADU installed in his backyard on Oakland Avenue for his mother to live in. “It was inconceivable that four or five [crew members] set the foundation up so quickly. They moved at light-speed,” said Villaluz at the time. Piedmont City Code allows properties with a single-family residence to have an ADU subject to provisions of City Code division 17.38. A detached one-bedroom ADU may be installed up to 850 square feet, must have independent exterior access, and cannot be taller than 16 feet. Accessory Dwelling Units have become popular in Piedmont as the city moves to meet its Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) goal of 587 units. An ADU is lifted by crane onto Mayor King’s backyard.

articles.text: Various groups in Piedmont have already begun celebrating and raising awareness for the 50th anniversary of the passage of Title IX legislation, which will occur on June 23. At the May 25 school board meeting the Piedmont Title IX Audit Task Force will present its finding which shows that high school girls’ sports have 55 fewer athletes than the boys. 91% of high school students play a sport and 78% of females play a sport. For those numbers to be equal, 55 more spots need to be made available for and filled by female high school students. Boys Girls PHS Athletes 406 332 Total PHS Students 446 425 % of Participants 91% 78% Title IX is considered by many to be the most important law for equal rights for women after the 1918 right to vote. In 1971-72, only 7% of U.S. high school athletes were girls. Now, girls comprise 43% of high school athletes. Title IX of The Education Amendments Act of 1972 states: “No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” The Task Force will also present the following research. Overall, girls who play sports have higher grades and score higher on standardized tests than non-athletes. Girls who participate in regular exercise experience lower rates of depression. A 2013 study by Ernst & Young of 821 senior managers and executives found that 94% of female executives played organized sports after primary school. Use this activity guide to explore rovers that humans have built, then design one of your own to explore a location in the solar system. Viper rover rolls into Chabot Starting on May 28, see a scale model of NASA’s Artemis lunar rover, the Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover, or VIPER. Launching in 2023, this rover is heading to the Moon’s South Pole in search of ice and other potential resources. Its 100- day mission will answer big questions about lunar water and how it can be used for future human space exploration. Learn more: https://chabot s p a c e.o r g /c a le n d a r / n a s a s - artemis-takeover/2022-05-28/. What is a rover? When humans want to learn about other planets or objects in the solar system, they can use tools like telescopes, satellites, and rovers. A rover is a small, mobile robot that scientists send to moons and planets to land on their surfaces and explore. Rovers can take pictures and collect information about the planet by taking temperature readings, rock, and soil samples. The rovers then send this information back to scientists on earth through radio signals. Rovers can help scientists learn about faraway places without having to send people to space, which can be tricky. Rover research NASA uses rovers to explore other places in our solar system. Research some of NASA’s past missions to learn about what rovers have in common, and how they can be different. Is NASA planning to send any rovers to space in the future? A rendering of NASA’s Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover, or VIPER sheet, sketch what you’d like your rover to look like. Optional Extension: Build a Prototype 1. Build the body of your rover. a) You can use a variety of materials for the body, but it should be something sturdy that you can attach other materials too. 2 Decorate the base. You can paint, color, or wrap your body however you’d like. 3. Build the wheels and legs of your rover. For help making a rover that rolls, follow steps (4-9) below. a) Materials that are round and can roll make great wheels. b) Straws are a helpful material if you’d like to build a rover that rolls. 4. Tape a straw, or cylinder of paper horizontally across the bottom of your rover. 5. Repeat with one, two, or three more straws/paper cylinders. Try to make them equally spaced out on your rover. 6. Identify the materials you will be using as wheels, and as axles. The axel will hold your two wheels together. a) You will need the same number of axles as paper cylinders or straws, and twice the number of wheels. 7. Thread the axle material through the straws or paper cylinders underneath your rover. 8. Use tape or glue to attach the center of your wheel to one end of an axle. Make sure the axel is still threaded through the straws on your rover. 9. Repeat so that each axle has two wheels attached to it, and is suspending on the bottom of your rover. 10. Add the arms, neck, and head to your rover. Use glue, tape, or poke them through the body of your rover to hold them in place. a) Strong, skinny materials that can stand up make good arms or necks. b) You can add different tools to the ends of your rover arms. 11. Add a brain, and an energy source to your rover. You can make them out of paper, cardboard, whatever material you think works best. 12. Decorate with logos, a flag, even passengers 13. When humans want to learn about other planets or objects in the solar system, they can use tools like telescopes, satellites, and rovers. A rover is a small, mobile robot that scientists send to moons and planets to land on their surfaces and explore. Rovers can take pictures and collect information about the planet by taking temperature readings, rock, and soil samples. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team was crowned once again as the Shoreline Division’s Western Alameda County champions on Friday, May 13 at the College of Alameda after beating Encinal 6-5 on Davis Alazraqui’s hard ground ball that caused an error, allowing Peter Krumins to score from second. The Highlanders rushed the field in celebration. It was Piedmont’s second WACC title in three attempts after last losing to Encinal 3-1 in the 2019 finals. It was coach Eric Olson’s third league championship victory. Friday’s meeting marked the third consecutive time the Highlanders and Jets faced one another for the league title. In 2018 Piedmont defeated Encinal 4-2 in the eighth inning. “This was the rubber match,” said Olson. “We played Encinal twice last week and knew that beating a team three times in a row is extremely difficult, it proved to be that way,” said Olson. Piedmont finished its regular season with an 18-8 overall record and 9-1 against league opponents. The Highlanders were 8-0 in 2021 but weren’t awarded a league banner due to the Covid-abbreviated season “I was just super happy that our kids got to experience success in the playoffs which they missed out on the last two seasons,” said Olson, a Piedmont native. Freshman center fielder Markos Lagios had a monster game, going 3-for-3 with a double, four RBIs, and a stolen base. “I always look forward to Markos’ at bats. He’s super competitive and has all the tools. Like any freshman on varsity, sometimes they try and do a little too much. We’ve wanted him to slow down in games, and we’re starting to see that. He’s had some big hits in the last few games,” said Olson. After the game, Piedmont shortstop Nico Defazio was awarded the Shoreline’s Most Valuable Player award alongside seven other All-League recipients: Alazraqui, Mike Aikawa, Tobin Cantrill, Will Sprague, Peter Krumins, and Alex Tafapolsky. The Highlanders, the no. 5 seed in the North Coast Section playoffs will square off with No. 12 St. Patrick today, May 18 at 5:00 p.m. Piedmont defeated the Bruins 3-2 on March 2. Game Recap Encinal led 3-1 following the top of the third inning and Piedmont narrowed the gap to 3-2 in the bottom of the fourth before Photo by Mike McConathy Piedmont players race onto the field to celebrate winning the league championship against Encinal. jumping ahead 5-3 in the bottom of the fifth. The Jets tied the game with one-run innings in the top of the sixth and seventh. The Highlanders and Alazraqui brought in the game-winner in the bottom of the seventh after a leadoff single by Krumins and five-pitch walk by Defazio. In Piedmont’s big fifth inning, the Highlanders loaded the bases with a leadoff walk by Aikawa, Krumins hitting a single, and Defazio drew a walk. With one Piedmont looks ahead to Wednesday’s opening round of the Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs as the No. 5 seed. articles.text: Piedmont High star swimmer Simon Lins is back from the CIF State Championship meet at Clovis West in Fresno on Friday and Saturday, May 13-14, where he competed in the 50 freestyle and 100 backstroke. He finished seventh of 18 in the freestyle by clocking a time of 20.44 in the finals, and was timed in 20.20 in the preliminaries, 2nd among 43 swimmers. Ethan Harrington of Palo Alto won with a State record in 19.85 seconds. “I knew going in that it would be really tight. I’m usually ahead on my dive and first breakout, but Ethan beat me in the underwater. It was a pleasure racing him and I’m looking forward to racing him again,” said Lins. Lins’ times qualified him for All-American honors. He entered the State meet after winning NCS’ 50 free with a time of 20.20 and was fifth in the 100 backstroke in 49.64. Lins also won the WACC Championship’s 50 free in 20.49 and had a time of 50.91 in the 100 Back. “I felt like I choked in the finals after being seeded second in the state for the 50. That morning I just felt [I wasn’t] in the right zone. I was looking to break 19 seconds and just wasn’t able to execute,” Lins said. He finished 12th of 16 in the finals of the backstroke with a time of 49.42. In the preliminaries, Lins was 12th of 39 with a slightly better time of 49.40. “In March, I got really sick and was unable to train for twoand-a-half weeks. I could barely eat or sleep, and couldn’t race. Come April, I was able to train and got back in racing ability. In January, I got COVID after winter break and was out for a few weeks; it put me in a bad place. And then right when I was starting to get back into racing shape, Simon Lins will compete over the summer with Piedmont Swim Team and has eyes on the Junior National in July. Photos by George White Simon Lins placed seventh of 18 in the CIF States’ 50 free finals and 12th of 16 in the 100 backstroke. His time of 20.44 in the finals and 20.20 in the preliminaries were fast enough to earn All-American honors. I got another bad virus. I couldn’t sleep and I couldn’t eat. But my coach and I were really patient about getting back into it, letting me go back through the steps of re-teaching my body to swim fast,” said Lins. Lins now moves into the summer swim season, where he will be competing with Piedmont Swim Team and coach Stefan Bill. He’ll be swimming in multiple events aiming for the Junior Nationals on July 28-31 in the Irvine Aquatics Center. “I’m going to work super hard this summer with my coach. I plan on attending Junior Nationals to get some high-quality racing in,” said Lins.

articles.text: The Highlander track team had a highly successful meet at the North Coast Section Bayshore sectional on Saturday, May 14 at Hayward High, with 11 PHS athletes in eight events earning topsix results. All qualified for the NCS Meet of Champions at Dublin High this Friday and Saturday, May 20-21. Jack Stein, Christian Taylor, Jamie Schwarz and Ellie Black qualified for the 1600 meters, and Black also qualified in the 3200 and plans to focus only on the 2-mile event. Cooper Downing and Schwarz qualified in the 800. The boys’ 4x100 relay team of Luke Alban, Quincy Munyan, Parker Terrill, and Matthew Riordan qualified for the MOC, in addition to the 4x400 team of Alban, Parker Long, Downing, and Terrill. Terrill will principally compete in the pole vault and 110-meter hurdles, and Brie Sotelo will compete in the shot. It’s the largest number of Piedmont athletes to qualify for the NCS Meet of Champions in five years. “It’s a great feeling. This team has really had a great season and had a lot of fun. I feel like this team is closer than other teams in all the disciplines, from the throws group, sprinters, and distance. It’s a really close group,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. Saturday was a memorable day for Downing, who won the 800 with a blazing time of 1:55.20 in a field of 21 runPhotos by Steve Zirkelbach Coach Jeanine Holmlund and Cooper Downing at the finish of the 4x400 relay. Downing won the 800 and helped the relay team finish second. Ellie Black qualified for the 3200 meters at the Meet of Champions. Parker Terrill qualified for the Meet of Champions in four events: pole vault, 110-meter hurdles, and 4x100 relay. ners. After finishing second to Berkeley’s Timothy Keller in the WACC Championship the previous week, Downing beat his opponent by .49 of a second. Downing also ran the anchor leg of the 4x400 relay which was second among 17 schools with a time of 3:27.915. Berkeley won in a photo finish by a razor-thin margin of .003 of a second. “Cooper is looking really good, and I still think he can run faster. His photo-finish in the relay was exhilarating to watch,” said Holmlund. Multi-event athlete Terrill qualified in three events. He won the pole vault with a height of 14 feet, 6 inches in a field of 14, finished fourth of 21 in the 110- meter hurdles in 16.99, and was on the 4x100 relay team. The 4x100 team of Terrill, Alban, Munyan, and Riordan was fourth of 15 teams with a time of 43.63. Holmlund credits Terrill’s presence as a decathlete as a key catalyst in the success of the team this season. Black finished second in both the 1600 and 3200, clocking 5:07.23 in the 1600 against 21 other runners, and posting a time of 11:14.08 in the 3200 in a field of 19. Schwarz, a sophomore, finished fifth in the 1600 in 5:23.63, and placed sixth of 22 in the 800 in 2:28.56. Sotelo was sixth in the shot with a distance of 27 feet, 10 inches. Stein finished second of 23 runners in the 1600 with a time of 4:17.93. He lost by .21 of a second to Alameda’s David Song after holding the lead over the Hornets’ runner until the last lap. Stein also competed in the 3200, and finished 10th in 10:02.34. It’s worth mentioning that Stein recently won the 1600 and 3200 at the WACC Championship ahead of Song, but Piedmont’s senior runner was dealing with an illness one week earlier, making his result in the 1600 an impressive accomplishment given his condition. Stein considers the 3200 his main event and holds the Piedmont school record in both the 1600 and 3200 meters. NEXT UP Piedmont heads to the NCS Meet of Champions in Dublin on Friday and Saturday, May 20-21. Events start 1:30 pm on Friday and 12:00 pm on Saturday. The top three finishers in each event qualify for the California State Meet at Buchanan High School in Clovis on Friday and Saturday, May 27-28.

articles.text: Piedmont’s tennis season came to an end on Saturday, May 14, with a tough 6-1 loss to No. 1 ranked Head-Royce in the Division 2 North Coast Section Team Tournament. The Highlanders entered as the No. 5 seed and upset No. 4 Lick Wilmerding 5-2 in the quarterfinals on Thursday, May 12 in San Francisco. Piedmont won its first-round match over No. 12 Sonoma Academy by forfeit due to a COVID-19 outbreak on the opposing team. The No. 1 Jayhawks went onto win the team title with a 5-2 win over No. 2 University of San Francisco. It marks the first NCS banner in Head-Royce school history. “Head-Royce is a very strong team. Although the score was lopsided, we put up a good fight.” said Piedmont coach Jim Landes. Piedmont was able to avenge a 4-3 loss to Lick Wilmerding on April 20 while playing in windy Golden Gate Park. This time, Piedmont controlled the day despite having three matches go to a third-set. “We beat Lick in the quarterfinals 5-2,” Landes said. “We played very well, winning three of four singles and two of three at doubles. There was a lot of tension when we were leading 3-1 with the three remaining matches going to a third set, but we took two of them.” Piedmont ended its season at 15-5 and earned this year’s Western Alameda County Conference banner after going a perfect 10-0 against league opponents. The Highlanders earned five All-League recipients, including Charlie Lambert, Ben Breber, and Lennie Burchardt at singles, and Kai Baudendistel and Charlie Olcott at doubles. 5-2 win over Lick Wilmerding Piedmont’s 5-2 victory started with two quick doubles wins, the No. 2 pairing of Monte Imburg and Charlie Sullivan winning 6-1, Staff Photos Monte Imburg won 6-1, 6-2 with Charlie Sullivan against Lick Wilmerding and 6-1, 6-4 over Head-Royce with Oliver Maxwell. 6-2, and No. 3 Brady Colbert and Oliver Maxwell winning 6-4, 6-4. In singles, Burchardt lost 6-4, 6-4 at No. 2, but Ethan Pham at No. 3 won 6-0, 7-5 to put Piedmont ahead 3-1. Charlie Lambert at No. 1 singles reeled in a three-set win to clinch the afternoon, 6-4, 4-6, 6-2. Also winning was Breber at No. 3 in three sets, 7-5, 4-6, 6-2. The No. 1 doubles team of Baudendistel and Olcott lost 5-7, 6-0, 6-2. 6-1 loss to Head-Royce Piedmont lost 6-1 to the eventual NCS champions in the semifinals on May 14 while playing at St. Mary’s College in Moraga. It was their second loss to HeadRoyce and by the same score this season. At doubles, Imburg and Oliver Maxwell claimed Piedmont’s only win of the day in straight sets at No. 2 by scores of 6-1, 6-4. At No. 1, Baudendistel and Olcott lost in three sets, 6-3, 3-6, 10-7. Sullivan and Jacob Hsia lost 6-4, 6-0 at No. 3. In singles, PHS lost all four matches in straight sets. Lambert lost 6-1, 6-3 at No. 1, Burchardt fell 6-2, 6-1 at No. 2, Breber lost 7-5, 6-3 at No. 3, and Pham lost 6-1, 6-2. Charlie Sullivan helped win at No. 2 doubles with Monte Imburg against Lick Wilmerding. At No. 1 singles, Charlie Lambert won in three sets against Lick Wilmerding.

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco currently is showing the “Memento: Jayashree Chakravarty and Lam Tung Pang” exhibit through June 6. The exhibition is part of an ongoing series of singular exhibitions at the museum entitled Today’s Asian Voices. The exhibition marks the inaugural Hambrecht Contemporary Gallery installation, which includes two contemporary works that speak to global issues of urbanization and political uncertainty. The Hambrecht Contemporary Gallery was formerly used for special exhibitions and has recently been transformed into a dedicated space for a rotating selection of both modern and contemporary works. Viewers will see Personal Space by Chakravarty (2001), an 8-foot-tall, 30-foot-wide work built from painted strips of paper. An immersive video by Hong Kong-based mixed media artist Pang entitled A Day of Two Suns (2019), combines unsynchronized images from four projectors that combine with the shadows of museum visitors and moving objects. “This work is prophetic and nostalgic,” said Abby Chen, Head of Contemporary Art about the newly acquired work. “It documents a city, and a system, in the process of fading and awakening.” For more information, visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/ exhibitions/memento-jayashreechakravarty-and-lam-tung-pang/. Asian Art Museum is located at 200 Larkin Street in San Francisco; phone (415) 581-3500. Personal Space, 2001, by Jayashree Chakravarty, currently on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco.
articles.title: Chakravarty and Pang exhibit at Asian Art Museum through June 6

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California’s exhibition celebrating Edith Heath, designer and founder of Heath Ceramics, is on display now through October 30. Edith Heath: A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist with over 50 pieces of ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video is shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artist’s career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. A Life in Clay was organized by Oakland Museum’s Curator of Photography Drew Johnson, and guest curator Jennifer Volland. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design,’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, OMCA is excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” (510) 652-1662 Office (510) 652-1690 Fax info@woodwindowswarehouse.com woodwindowswarehouse.com 1301 66th Street Emeryville, CA 94608 Wood Windows Warehouse Residential & Commercial Custom & Standard CA Contractors License No. 823258 Edith Heath, founder of Heath Ceramics A Life in Clay examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than fifty years ago is now a modern-day classic,” said Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To learn more about the exhibition, and to purchase tickets, visit www.museumca.org.
articles.title: Edith Heath’s Life in Clay exhibit at Oakland Museum through Oct. 30

articles.text: Mountain Theatre’s production of Hello Dolly opens this Sunday, May 22 on Mt. Tamalpais above Mill Valley. Hello, Dolly!, the blockbuster Broadway hit, bursts with humor, romance, high-energy dancing, and some of the greatest songs in musical theater history. The romantic and comic exploits of Dolly Gallaher-Levi, turn-of-the-century matchmaker and “woman who arranges things,” are certain to entertain audiences of all ages. Starring Dyan McBride as Mrs. Dolly Gallagher Levi and Randy Nazarian, as Horace Vandergelder, the production includes Miranda Long, a sophomore at Piedmont High School, in the ensemble. Long is the only cast member under 17 years old and is thrilled to make her Mountain Play debut. Jerry Herman’s feel-good score includes such memorable songs as “Put on Your Sunday Clothes,” “Ribbons Down My Back,” “Before the Parade Passes By,” “Elegance,” “It Only Takes a Moment,” and the title song “Hello, Dolly.” This one-of a kind mountaintop event takes place at Cushing Memorial Amphitheatre, better known as the Mountain Theatre, an open-air venue in Mount Tamalpais State Park with 3750 seats. It has redwood groves and oak woodlands with a spectacular view from its 2,571-foot peak. On a clear day, visitors can see the Farallon Islands 25 miles out to sea, the Marin County hills, San Francisco and the bay, hills, and cities of the East Bay, and Mount Diablo. The musical will be performed at 2 p.m. on May 22 and 29, and June 5, 11, 12 and 19. For tickets, visit mountainplay.org.

articles.text: Opera and theater, from Greek tragedy to those 18th Century rock stars the Castrati, have historically told stories through a broad spectrum of voices, personalities, and gender expressions. Performed and curated by mezzo-soprano Lily Bogas and countertenor Matheus Coura, They Sing! will be performed at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, May 22 at 5 p.m. Explore feelings from sublime to irreverent to comedic: recognizing that voices of the same range have validity in roles across the gender spectrum. This program will feature arias, songs, and duets by Monteverdi, Handel, Mozart, Bizet, Strauss, Kurt Weill, and Ricky Ian Gordon. They Sing! will take you on a journey through the past, present and into the future of how music has shaped and reflected the multifaceted human experience. Mezzo soprano Lily Bogas is a student at the Eastman School of Music, Her recent credits include Taller Daughter in Missy Mazzoli’s Proving Up, Dido in Dido and Aeneas, and Cinderella in Into the Woods. A finalist in the National CS Vocal Competition, and third place winner in the Schmidt Vocal Competition, Bogas was also a finalist in the American Songbook Academy, performing jazz standards alongside Michael Feinstein. Bogas will be making her mainstage debut with Festival Opera as Clotilde in Norma this season. Praised for his “sonorous voice” and “delightful spontaneity”, Brazilian-American countertenor Matheus Coura’s recent performances include Giuliano in Eliogabalo with West Edge Opera, and Narcissus in Two united in a single soul with San Francisco Ballet. Coura is a recipient of the SF Artist Grant, was a finalist in the Bethlehem Bach Competition, and was a prize winner at the St. Petersburg Opera Guild and Cooper-Bing Competitions. Coura is also an international portrait photographer, and resident artist at The Convent Arts Collective where he co-founded the drag revue Bad Habits. Poster for They Sing!

My question to you is: “are the most famous musicians on the international concert circuit really the best?“ It is an ongoing question, and open to constant review. It was a busy weekend of four concerts in three days. On Friday evening the San Francisco Philharmonic played a gala concert in Herbst Theater. They are one of the newer ensembles and are trying to establish a niche. These days, many musical organizations send out “subliminal messages“ in order to secure a fan base. Philharmonic seems to be in alliance with this philosophy. My interest is purely musical. I need to state this unequivocally. In my opinion, Philharmonic is a high level musical ensemble. They play well, despite some shortcomings in membership. Their conductor, Jessica Bejarano, is an inspiration and encourages the players to play above their ability. That is what matters to me and, to be honest with you, that is what matters to the music. Philharmonic‘s assets are: 1) a conductor who inspires the best effort in the players and the music. And 2) A supportive and enthusiastic audience. The evening’s concert had an added bonus…a cello soloist who is worthy of a worldwide solo career.

articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Michael Friedes, an artist and interior designer, is having his debut art exhibition at Piedmont Center for the Arts. Margaret O’Hagan’s style was further informed by Picasso and the indigenous people of the Pacific Northwest. Andy’s early work reflects her teacher’s influences. articles.text: On Thursday, May 12, Piedmont High School art students showcased their masterpieces from throughout the year at the All-School Art Show. The exhibit was on view from 6:00-8:00 p.m. in the new theater building foyer, the second such event in the building. More than 200 students from Art 1-4, Ceramics 1-4, Digital Design and Digital Photography entered pieces. The exhibit included 300 pieces. Sophomore Taylor Rolefson’s piece contrasts the world of color with that of black and white. The May 12 Art show gave every Piedmont High School art student the opportunity to display 1-3 pieces. “It was a wonderful celebration of their work. So many artists were there and received support from friends, family, and community members,” said PHS Art teacher Gillian Bailey. All art students at PHS and MHS were represented in the show, except for AP students, who had their own show two weeks earlier. Junior Henry Brayer explained the lessons he learned from Ceramics teacher Hannah Bjork to create his teapot. “I’m usually pressing the clay down really hard and trying to muscle it, but clay is much more delicate. Ms. Bjork showed me a lot of ways to maneuver your way around the clay. She says don’t fight the clay, use the clay to your advantage and don’t try to force anything to it.” The Introduction class, Art 1, created pieces which focused on a color background and moved from the back to front, by trying to develop form with a small object. Hot sauce labels and food Hailey Ronin’s newspaper ship literally sails off the page. Art teacher Department Chair Gillian Bailey stands by a taco truck project constructed from photopaper. trucks were made by the Digital Design students, requiring not only the design, but production of the label for sauce bottles and miniature trucks folded from photo paper. A 3D-Art class focused pieces on textures of underwater landscapes. Another favorite project of Art 2 was the shoe project, producing fine representations of student’s prized Converse, Nike and high heel footwear. In one of Bjork’s ceramics classes, her students were challenged to produced 2-D aerial views of their homes and a ceramic 3-D piece accompanying. This was their first gallery showing in high school for many students. The last one was in 2019. “During the pandemic some kids really flourished in art, but some kids really felt locked down. If you don’t have emotional energy trying to do creative things and break out if that is not a natural outlet for you, it can be very tough,” said Bailey. Sophomore Bauer Peterson used acrylic paint to produce the largest piece in the show measuring 3 x 5 feet.

articles.text: In honor of Asian American Pacific Islander Heritage Month, join a special screening of Far East Deep South followed by a discussion with the producer/ director. The event will be virtual. • May 21-24 Film Screening (on demand) • May 23, 7 p.m. A discussion with producer Baldwin Chiu and director Larissa Lam, moderated by Bryant Lin. The screening is sponsored by Stanford Center for Asian Health Research and Education, and the Vincent V. C. Woo Memorial Foundation, in partnership with the American Medical Women’s Association and Piedmont Asian American Club. About the film Far East Deep South follows Charles Chiu and his family as they travel from California to Mississippi to find the grave of Charles’ father, K.C. Lou. Their search leads to stunning revelations about their family and they get a crash course on the history of Chinese immigrants in the segregated South. Through encounters with local residents and historians, this Chinese American family not only discovers their family’s important role in the Mississippi Delta, but they also learn about the symbiotic relationship between the Black and Chinese communities during the Jim Crow era. The film provides a window into the struggles of Chinese immigrants in the American South during the late 1800s to mid-1900s and the discrimination they faced. The Chiu family’s history demonstrates how exclusionary immigration laws like the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 separated their family for generations. This deeply moving and unforgettable story offers a poignant and important perspective on race relations, immigration and American identity. For more information visit www.fareastdeepsouth.com.

articles.text: It’s an interesting experience to approach a film with one set of expectations and realize, as the story evolves, that it is entirely something else. That’s the case of Mr. Holmes. Going in I assumed that the setting would be London, during those nascent years of the 20th century, not long after the end of World War I. Mr. Holmes is at the top of his deductive game and often takes intricate cases with subtle clues to be cleverly unraveled. Buttressing my assumption is the fact that Ian McKellen, a gifted character actor, is portraying Holmes, sans deerstalker cap and oversized Meerschaum pipe (something Watson added), but in all ways a perfectly cast Holmes. But Mr. Holmes is a different movie. Based on the novel A Slight Trick of the Mind, by Mitch Cullin, the narrative is set in 1947. Sherlock Holmes, now in his 90s, is living on his bucolic Sussex farm. He has been retired for some 30 years and has used this time to raise bees and study botany. He lives a solitary life, with the exception of his housekeeper, Mrs. Munro (Laura Linney), and her precocious 10-yearold son, Roger (Milo Parker). As is soon made evident, Mr. Holmes is a penetrating character study of a man once renowned, thanks to the embellished writings of his friend and case collaborator, Dr. John H. Watson, who wrote what Holmes refers to as “penny dreadfuls” about their exploits. He has retreated from his former life and is now confronted with the harsh realities of aging – his once keen mind going sideways, his powers of observation, always the fulcrum of his detection, growing increasingly elusive. Holmes is gradually becoming a man who has outlived the person he once cherished: his former self. His daily frustration with his decline, compounded by regret for certain choices from his past, has made him taciturn and even a bit desperate. At one point, his face folding in emotional pain, he acknowledges, “I have been alone all of my life.” There is one seemingly minor case offered up through flashbacks, relevant because it causes Holmes such pain that its conclusion results in his retirement. He remembers only that the year was 1919 and it involved a recently married woman (Hattie Morahan) who was enamored with learning to play the glass harmonica. Against her husband’s wishes. Holmes is hired to follow her and discover how she is paying for her lessons. What he can’t sort out is what occurred that caused him to leave his flourishing practice and move to Sussex 30 years ago from London. With the encouragement of Roger, who has clandestinely read the initial pages, Holmes tries to write down the details of the case, hoping to puzzle out its denouement. Meanwhile, he is also in search of a restorative herb that will revitalize his mind as well as his body. He makes a journey to Hiroshima, Japan, but to no avail. What makes Mr. Holmes worthwhile is the exceptional performance of Ian McKellen. He is, in every respect, Sherlock Holmes. In the backstory we see a face that is a study in incisive intelligence and vitality, his style incomparable. It’s only later that he falls into a kind of helpless sadness and longs for what once was. McKellen is, in a word, remarkable in both roles. Mr. Holmes. Starring Ian McKellen, Laura Linney and Milo Parker. Directed by Bill Condon. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG. Released in 2015. Review published in the Post in 2015. Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple TV.

articles.text: Bouquets to Art, the de Young Museum’s premiere fundraiser and annual display of artwork-inspired floral installations, will begin on June 7. Bouquets to Art, now in its 38th year, is back to full-capacity following a virtual event in 2020 and a hybrid, limited-capacity event last year. For one week, more than 100 experienced floral designers will converge at the de Young to showcase arrangements inspired by the museum’s vast array of paintings, sculptures, and architecture. Bouquets to Art is one of the Fine Arts Museum of San Francisco’s most popular and well-attended events every year. The event is presented by the volunteer members of the fine arts museums - and draws nearly 800,000 visitors a year, with net proceeds of more than $7 million. Funds from the event help underwrite special exhibitions, conservation projects, and educational programming. Guests will be greeted with a large-scale aerial artwork piece by Bay Area artist Windy Chien. Entitled The Three Dragons, the hand-knotted artwork hangs in the museum’s Wilsey Court. Those who visit during the week of Bouquets to Art will have a chance to view Hung Liu’s large piece Resident Alien, first exhibited at the Capp Street Project in 1988 and exhibited by the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco last year. The painting, arguably Liu’s most famous, depicts her own “Green Card” on a larger-than-life scale. It is now in the collection of the San Jose Museum of Art. “Hung Liu is uniquely positioned to tell the stories of immigrants to the United States. In 2020, she celebrated the milestone of having lived an equal number of years in China and the United States. As one of the foremost painters in the United States, Liu is a testament to the fact that our brightest citizens are often born under foreign skies,” said Janna Keegan, Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art and Programming at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Bouquets to Art is a weeklong event that officially kicks off on the evening of June 6 with an opening-night party. Between June 7 and June 12, a series of lectures, book launches, and raffles will take place. For a full list of programming, visit https:// www.famsf.org/press-room/bouquets-art. Tickets sold out weeks prior to the event in 2021. Reserve your tickets now by visiting https:// deyoung.famsf.org/bouquets-toart. Bouquets to Art in 2010. Photo by Yuri Krasov

Buttressing my assumption is the fact that Ian McKellen, a gifted character actor, is portraying Holmes, sans deerstalker cap and oversized Meerschaum pipe (something Watson added), but in all ways a perfectly cast Holmes. But Mr. Holmes is a different movie. Based on the novel A Slight Trick of the Mind, by Mitch Cullin, the narrative is set in 1947. Sherlock Holmes, now in his 90s, is living on his bucolic Sussex farm. He has been retired for some 30 years and has used this time to raise bees and study botany. He lives a solitary life, with the exception of his housekeeper, Mrs. Munro (Laura Linney), and her precocious 10-yearold son, Roger (Milo Parker). As is soon made evident, Mr. Holmes is a penetrating character study of a man once renowned, thanks to the embellished writings of his friend and case collaborator, Dr. John H. Watson, who wrote what Holmes refers to as “penny dreadfuls” about their exploits. He has retreated from his former life and is now confronted with the harsh realities of aging – his once keen mind going sideways, his powers of observation, always the fulcrum of his detection, growing increasingly elusive. Holmes is gradually becoming a man who has outlived the person he once cherished: his former self. His daily frustration with his decline, compounded by regret for certain choices from his past, has made him taciturn and even a bit desperate. At one point, his face folding in emotional pain, he acknowledges, “I have been alone all of my life.” There is one seemingly minor case offered up through flashbacks, relevant because it causes Holmes such pain that its conclusion results in his retirement. He remembers only that the year was 1919 and it involved a recently married woman (Hattie Morahan) who was enamored with learning to play the glass harmonica. Against her husband’s wishes. Holmes is hired to follow her and discover how she is paying for her lessons. What he can’t sort out is what occurred that caused him to leave his flourishing practice and move to Sussex 30 years ago from London. With the encouragement of Roger, who has clandestinely read the initial pages, Holmes tries to write down the details of the case, hoping to puzzle out its denouement. Meanwhile, he is also in search of a restorative herb that will revitalize his mind as well as his body. He makes a journey to Hiroshima, Japan, but to no avail. What makes Mr. Holmes worthwhile is the exceptional performance of Ian McKellen. He is, in every respect, Sherlock Holmes. In the backstory we see a face that is a study in incisive intelligence and vitality, his style incomparable. It’s only later that he falls into a kind of helpless sadness and longs for what once was. McKellen is, in a word, remarkable in both roles. Mr. Holmes. articles.text: After an incredible two years of triumph and transition during the pandemic, Stagebridge, the East Bay’s longest running and most renowned performing arts organization for older adults, welcomes the return to in-person classes with its popular Performing Arts Camp this June. “I’m excited to see the students return to Stagebridge, to see how much they enjoy the classes, and to see what they can accomplish with the performances they create,” said Outreach Coordinator Barbara Johnson. T he su m mer ca mp is designed to introduce Stagebridge’s lifelong learning programs to students 50 years and older. The two-week session will showcase some of the talented teaching artists, many of whom joined Stagebridge as a part of distance learning programming. The camp will feature local and national phenoms, such as poet Tony Aldarondo, global dance and movement leader April Axé Charmaine, theatre performer Andy Alabran, and Heidi Carlsen of American Conservatory Theater. “At the start of the pandemic, Stagebridge was forced to embrace online learning, which was particularly challenging given the population we serve,” explained Elissa Glickman, Stagebridge’s new Managing Director. “For a community in complete isolation, Stagebridge was a connective lifeline, a hub of creative expression.” “When I arrived two months ago, everyone asked when we’d return to in-person learning. Building upon the past, Stagebridge will re-introduce the company’s flagship community service program, Seniors Reaching Out, in addition to showcasing full-length productions created by students. In 2021, instructors Scrumbly Koldewyn and Joanne Grimm led students in creating The Dell, following fictional and fairytale characters fighting against a developer threatening to tear down their home. My Dear Readers: One of my clients, Linda, called me and described how she was taken for several hundred dollars by one of the many tech-support scams that are going around. This is what happened to her. She woke up and turned her computer on, and started checking her email, checking the news websites that she usually does, and all of a sudden, a screen appeared, with a very loud alarm noise and message indicating that she had a virus. Call this number now, toll free 1-800-xxx-xxxx” WARNING! DO NOT SHUT DOWN YOUR COMPUTER!” Since the pop-up window indicated that the number that she was going to call would be Apple support, but pf course it wasn’t, she called it right away. They sent her a small application so they could log onto her computer and showed her some very scary looking files. They said that they were malware and that she would have to act immediately so that they could clean her system of any viruses. They said that because they had a security protocol in place, she could pay them with a credit card, but she would have to authenticate that with a bank account, and her Social Security number. She gave them the credit card number, she also gave them her checking account routing number and account number, she was about to give them her Social Security number when her roommate came into the room and said to her, “What are you doing!?” She realized that she was being By Benjamin and Leah Bloom May is Older Americans Month, a recognition promoted by the Administration for Community Living. The theme changes from year to year and this time it is a focus on aging in place titled, “Age My Way.” It is described as a way to show how older adults can plan to stay in their homes and live independently in their communities for as long as possible. The Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) defines aging in place as, “the ability to live in one’s own home and community safely, independently, and comfortably, regardless of age, income, or ability level.” Under any definition of aging in place, there is a mention of support, Seniors scammed, and told Linda to shut off her computer and hang up immediately. When the scammer heard the roommate telling her to shut the computer off, yelled at her and said, “No! If you shut your computer down, all of the virus files will reload when you start it up again!” Linda was obviously frightened and froze. Her roommate ran over to the computer and turned it off. At this point, the scammer on the phone called them both some colorful names and hung up. But not before Linda was out about $700. She called me after this happened, and I told her to call her bank and credit card immediately and try to block the charges. She was able to recover all but about $250. This was a very expensive lesson, and Linda was incredibly shaken by the experience. She was worried about losing the contents of her computer, as she is finishing a PhD and she felt that all her work was at stake. Linda is a very smart woman, but the cunning of this scammer took advantage of her fear of losing her precious data. There are so many of these types of scams going around, sometimes by email, sometimes by phone calls, and sometimes like this with a pop up on your computer. In many cases they convince their targets to pay by gift cards and of course credit cards. How to avoid scams There are two things you should know about how to avoid these scams: 1. Microsoft, Apple, or any legitimate tech company will not contact you by phone, email, text or pop up that there is something wrong with your computer. 2. And not all security pop-ups are scams, but no legitimate one will ever give you a phone number to call. What to do if you think you have been scammed 1. Call your bank immediately, call your credit card immediately and if you have been the victim of a gift card scam, where the scammers asked you to pay by Amazon gift card, call Amazon customer support and let them know you have been a victim of fraud. They may be able to invalidate the card and refund your money 2. You can report the scammer to ReportFraud.ftc.gov. 3. Change your password at your bank if you have a password to access your credit card. If you are the victim of a gift card fraud, change your password with that company. 4. Be very careful about clicking on links in email messages, or in text messages. Tell your friends not to send you links to newspaper articles, etc. If you want to look something up, go to the newspaper website and look up the subject or the article in question. 5. Make sure your operating system is up to date. If you feel it’s necessary, install security software on your computer. If you’re a MacUser, I recommend Malwarebytes. Of course, security software will not prevent scammers from sending you phishing emails. 6. If your computer is too old to receive security updates, consider purchasing a new machine. You can block the pop-up windows on the browser you were using and only enable them if you are filling out a form that requires a pop-up to complete. It’s obvious that these types of scams are not going away, so, it’s important that you remain vigilant, and informed. As more and more people put precious data on computers, on the Internet, and in the cloud, we are all vulnerable to being hacked. Computers have made our lives easier in some ways, but we must always be careful not to fall prey to these ruthless scammers. articles.text: Wednesday, April 20 was another day of exploration by the Piedmont Seniors group, as 19 members ventured halfway to San Francisco to learn more of the city’s history. Their first stop was a visit to Treasure Island, which is currently undergoing extensive construction. Huge boulders from the original construction of the Caldecott Tunnel are strategically placed on the side of the main road. Treasure Island. Located on Yerba Buena Island in the middle of San Francisco Bay, offers a breathtaking view of the San Francisco skyline. On their visit, the Seniors also witnessed a new ferry terminal, which recently opened. The terminal will be particularly valuable when the residential housing and redevelopment is completed. The first stop was the Treasure Island Museum, founded by the U.S. Navy in 1975. The museum occupies the lobby of one of the original airport buildings constructed in 1937. and is protected on the National Register of Historic Places. Its claim to fame is that it served as the administrative center for the Golden Gate International Exposition (the World Fair in 1939, and also for Pan American Airways, and headquarters for the Twelfth Naval District. The museum originally was an Allied Navy, Marine, and Coast Guard Museum. It has an outElene Manolis in front of the Islands of the Pacific statue created for the Golden Gate International Exposition on Yerba Buena Island in 1938. standing mural on the museum’s back wall measuring 251 feet long and 26 feet high, representing scenes in the history of the Navy and Marine Corps in the Pacific since 1813. The Golden Gate International Exposition of 1939-1940, also known as the “Pageant of the Pacific” was a glowing Art Deco island of towers, gardens, goddesses, and dazzling lighting effects to celebrate California and San Francisco as an economic, political, and cultural force in the Pacific region. At that time San Francisco was also celebrating the engineering achievements of the completion of both the Golden Gate and Bay Bridges. There was even the controversial Sally Rand Nude Ranch on the island featuring the well publicized stripper, and creating quite a stir. In addition, visitors could see the first “incubator babies” and even Botticelli’s “Birth of Venus” on display. These exhibits were in addition to the carnival rides and traditional booths one might see at an international fair. However, as America prepared for World War II, the island became a major training, supply, and embarkation station for American military efforts throughout the Pacific and Asia. Piedmont Seniors learn more San Francisco history By Janet Epstein Wednesday, April 20 was another day of exploration by the Piedmont Seniors group, as 19 members ventured halfway to San Francisco to learn more of the city’s history. Their first stop was a visit to Treasure Island, which is currently undergoing extensive construction. Huge boulders from the original construction of the Caldecott Tunnel are strategically placed on the side of the main road. Treasure Island. Located on Yerba Buena Island in the middle of San Francisco Bay, offers a breathtaking view of the San Francisco skyline. On their visit, the Seniors also witnessed a new ferry terminal, which recently opened. The terminal will be particularly valuable when the residential housing and redevelopment is completed. The first stop was the Treasure Island Museum, founded by the U.S. Navy in 1975. The museum occupies the lobby of one of the original airport buildings constructed in 1937. and is protected on the National Register of Historic Places. Its claim to fame is that it served as the administrative center for the Golden Gate International Exposition (the World Fair in 1939, and also for Pan American Airways, and headquarters for the Twelfth Naval District. The museum originally was an Allied Navy, Marine, and Coast Guard Museum. It has an outElene Manolis in front of the Islands of the Pacific statue created for the Golden Gate International Exposition on Yerba Buena Island in 1938. standing mural on the museum’s back wall measuring 251 feet long and 26 feet high, representing scenes in the history of the Navy and Marine Corps in the Pacific since 1813. The Golden Gate International Exposition of 1939-1940, also known as the “Pageant of the Pacific” was a glowing Art Deco island of towers, gardens, goddesses, and dazzling lighting effects to celebrate California and San Francisco as an economic, political, and cultural force in the Pacific region. At that time San Francisco was also celebrating the engineering achievements of the completion of both the Golden Gate and Bay Bridges. There was even the controversial Sally Rand Nude Ranch on the island featuring the well publicized stripper, and creating quite a stir. In addition, visitors could see the first “incubator babies” and even Botticelli’s “Birth of Venus” on display. These exhibits were in addition to the carnival rides and traditional booths one might see at an international fair. However, as America prepared for World War II, the island became a major training, supply, and embarkation station for American military efforts throughout the Pacific and Asia. articles.text: As a small boy I remember my grandmother’s talent for arts and crafts. I would sit while she attempted to teach me how to do whatever project she was working on. Whether it was making beautiful beaded ornaments for a Christmas tree, hand-made lace doilies or embroidering napkins, I was mesmerized. Over the years I’ve heard people say, “I think I’ll take up watercolors when I retire” or “Learning how to make pottery in my later years has been exhilarating.” I can’t help but wonder if there is a correlation between finally having the time to create and the benefits that could affect our well-being. Studies show that engaging in creative art pursuits provide older adults with multiple benefits, not the least of which is enhanced cognitive function. Scientists examining the engagement of older adults with art therapy and music therapy confirm that art can affect them in very positive ways. Exercising our creative selves can often induce psychological and physiological healing, while nurturing overall well-being. And it’s fun. Gene Cohen, MD, PhD, director of the Center on Aging at George Washington University, was the first researcher to conduct a national study on art and the quality of life. He found that engagement with the arts has a positive effect on health and illness as we age. The benefits are there for both the creator and viewer. Some of these benefits include helping individuals relax, assisting in socialization, encouraging playfulness and a sense of Oakland painter and poet Charles Blackwell humor. The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living boasts a large group of residents who are artists. Pat K. (pictured) has been painting all her life. She told me she chose her apartment in our community because the kitchen has a lake view and she set it up as an art studio. Jon C. has been drawing for over sixty years. He currently has a collection of his sketches on exhibit at The Lake Merritt from the present day dating back to 1946. Jon said he looks forward to our weekly open art studio where he can draw in the company of others and share creative ideas with fellow artists. Another resident, Pat R. has dabbled with different art forms throughout her life. She said, “Now that I am retired, I have so much more time for art, and I believe it’s good for my soul.” Many of our residents share a love of art and that’s what drives some of the programs at The Lake Merritt. We visit Bay Area arts and crafts exhibits, open art studios, take art history courses and make regular trips to museums and galleries. As for me, I am inspired by the many talented artists at The Lake Merritt, and though I won’t equal their caliber, when I retire I think I’ll take up watercolors. How about you? On this theme, we are particularly excited to offer a FREE Zoom presentation by Oakland painter and poet Charles Blackwell entitled, “Painting Beyond Vision” on May 26 at 3:30 p.m.. An artist since a young age, Blackwell suffered an accident that damaged his eyes and is now legally blind. When he lost most of his eyesight, his doctor told him, “Take your defect and make it an asset.” Blackwell has grown to embody this phrase. He creates art using acrylic paints, ink and canvas by leaning in very close to see the canvas through his limited peripheral vision. Blackwell has been the subject of a documentary film The God Given Talent and was featured recently in a profile by the San Francisco Chronicle. We’re thrilled to host this talented and uplifting artist in our Topics of Merritt series. The public is invited to join us by registering at https://tinyurl.com/ beyondvision or you may call 510-903-3600 for more information. articles.text: Gloria (Gabriel) Lawler, a Piedmont resident for 55 years, passed away on May 1 after a year-long battle with uterine cancer. She was 85 years old. Gloria grew up in a tight-knit Italian family outside of Philadelphia. She was an exceptional student in the Lower Merion school system and won a full scholarship to Rosemont College. While at Rosemont, she met Kaz Lawler, an ensign in the U.S. Navy, who attended nearby Villanova University. Shortly after her graduation from Rosemont with honors in Chemistry, Gloria and Kaz married. She and Kaz then made the first of many moves in the U.S. with the Navy, and along the way, they started their family. The couple and their five children eventually landed in Piedmont, California, where they have lived for 55 years. At a time when women were scarce in the Sciences, Gloria was a STEM pioneer and advocate for women in technology. After some time as a chemist for the FDA, Gloria became a technical writing innovator for chemical informatics start-ups, as well as a valued contributor to the scientific missions of Lawrence Berkeley Lab, Stanford Research Institute, and Lawrence Livermore Lab. In addition to raising her five children and working full-time, Gloria was active in the community, holding board positions and working to advance early childhood education. Following retirement, Gloria became the volunteer publicist for the Youth Musical Theater Company in Berkeley, writing theater reviews for the Piedmont Post. After their last child graduated from college, Gloria and Kaz hit the road and traveled around the Gloria Lawler died on May 1 after a year-long battle with cancer. She was 85. globe. Gloria loved traveling and visited 25 countries. France was a favorite, particularly Paris. Over the years, she and Kaz joyfully introduced each of their eight grandchildren to this magical city. Gloria is survived by her husband of almost 64 years, Kaz; her children Ann (Steve), MaryJo, Kaz Jr (Anne), Bob (Shannon), and Dave (Saroja). She is also survived by grandchildren Mike, Katherine, Andy (Rocky), Gates (Ben), Glynnis (Andy), Finn, Shayla, and Karina. Additionally she is survived by brother Michael Gabriel and sister Veronica Gabriel; nieces Sandy Mayson and Sarah Jo Mayson, and nephew Joe Gabriel. A memorial service will be held on June 3 at 11 a.m. in the Tower Chapel at Mountain View Cemetery, 5000 Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. The family suggests that memorial donations may be made to The American Cancer Society at www.cancer.org.

articles.text: Customers to see 8% drought surcharge on July 1 East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) announced on April 26 a district-wide “Stage 2 Drought Emergency”, following the driest January to March period on record. A “Stage 2” drought is triggered when EDMUD reservoirs fall below 75%; currently, reservoirs are 71% full. “Despite a strong rainy start in October and December, the dry winter has compelled us to move into our next phase of action to ensure we have adequate supplies in case the drought continues next year,” EBMUD Board President Douglas Linney said. “We’ve spent decades planning and preparing for these events and are confident our efforts, combined with customer water savings, will get us through this drought.” The EBMUD Board voted 6-1 to mandate a 10 percent district-wide water use reduction target, which affects Piedmont residents. EBMUD serves 1.4 million customers. Declaring a Stage 2 drought ensures the water utility meets the needs of its customers if the dry weather continues, explained Linney. Board members also voted to impose an 8% surcharge for all customers beginning July 1, in an attempt to offset costs due to the drought. “We are making the best use of all our tools to handle the drought, including purchasing water from partner agencies, increasing conservation from customers, and discouraging waste among high-volume users,” Linney said. “These emergency actions are outside our normal scope of work, and this drought surcharge will help us cover a portion of these costs.” The Board reinstated an excessive use penalty ordinance charged to households that use more than 1,600 gallons per day. The agency will issue one warning, then charge $2 for every 748 gallons used above the penalty threshold if not amended. The agency also updated restrictions on outdoor water use - outdoor watering is now limited to three times per week. is about the entire World War II, as is the Bayeux Museum. The Falaise Memorial follows the path of what it was like for the civilian population in wartime. Le Grand Bunker features the plight of the Sword Beach invasion along a section of the dangerous Atlantic Wall, heavily booby-trapped by the Germans. Remembrance Day, June 6, is shared by France, England, and the U.S. every year. Thousands of veterans are still alive. A “Stage 2” drought is triggered when EDMUD reservoirs fall below 75%; currently, reservoirs are 71% full. “Despite a strong rainy start in October and December, the dry winter has compelled us to move into our next phase of action to ensure we have adequate supplies in case the drought continues next year,” EBMUD Board President Douglas Linney said. “We’ve spent decades planning and preparing for these events and are confident our efforts, combined with customer water savings, will get us through this drought.” The EBMUD Board voted 6-1 to mandate a 10 percent district-wide water use reduction target, which affects Piedmont residents. EBMUD serves 1.4 million customers. Declaring a Stage 2 drought ensures the water utility meets the needs of its customers if the dry weather continues, explained Linney.
